interactions.summary: Jiang asks whether the Divine Comedy can resemble psychedelic revelation; students argue both that the states are not directly comparable and that many trip endpoints converge on the truth the poem states more clearly.

Jiang pivots to intense religious experience, and a student recounts a month of hell-like nightmares in Malaysia that ended only when Bible verses and the name of Jesus were invoked, leading to conversion.

speaker_notes.note: The student's language is emotionally raw and profane; preserve the force of conviction without mistaking it for a general doctrinal proof.

claims.claim: Jiang suggests the Divine Comedy may produce a consciousness comparable to psychedelics if read with sufficient total commitment rather than superficially.
A student says psychedelic revelation often ends at a truth the Divine Comedy states with greater clarity, while personal trips are flawed rewritings filtered through personality.
A student testifies that recurrent nightmares and a felt encounter with hell ended only through Christian verbal invocation, which became the decisive basis for conversion.
claims.temporal_scope: Student biographical testimony described in class on 2026-06-24.

signature_moments.moment: A mushroom trip is described as a cracked personal refraction of a truth the poem already holds in crystal clarity.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves one of the sharpest metaphors in the whole experiential sequence.

signature_moments.moment: Hell becomes existentially undeniable to the student because the only exit from the nightmares was screaming the name of Jesus.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i had to scream the name of Jesus
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows the class moving from literary discussion into explicit conversion testimony.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's category for firsthand experiences that push spiritual questions from theory into lived certainty.

chronology_notes.note: The discussion escalates here from comparative altered states into explicit conversion narrative, making the poem a bridge between literary interpretation and religious testimony.
